messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tui was eight years old when the violence began—always after his father arrived home on his bicycle, the smell of alcohol hitting the door before he did. That sound, the thud of fists against his mother’s body, the crash of furniture, the way she crumpled silent afterwards, lodged in him as a fragmented set of snapshots: the bicycle wheel spinning in the hallway, the empty bottle rolling, his mother’s hand reaching for nothing. He never saw the whole event in his mind; what returned were disconnected pieces that carried the same raw terror he had felt then, leaving him shaking and disoriented for hours afterward. As a teenager, he learned that riding his own bike past a bar or catching a whiff of beer on someone’s breath could trigger those memory fragments to surface without warning, the terror hitting him fresh even though years had passed.

Now eighteen and working as a project manager at a small construction firm, Tui finds his days shaped by a constant watchfulness he cannot turn off. He checks meeting rooms for exits, positions himself with his back to the wall, and watches his male colleagues—particularly the ones who joke about after-work drinks—for any shift in tone or posture that might signal danger. The alcohol smell that sometimes clings to a coworker’s jacket is enough to send his attention skittering, and when that happens, the incomplete memories of his father’s rages press in: the disconnected flashes, the terror, the sense that something terrible is about to happen again. In response, he starts smoking more, steps outside for a cigarette even when he doesn’t want one, and sometimes drinks a beer alone at lunch to dampen the edge. He has come to believe that if he stays vigilant—if he keeps checking doors, if he startles at every sudden sound—he might be able to detect a threat before it reaches him. But the avoidance of other people, the way he turns down invitations and leaves early, isolates him; his girlfriend has begun to ask why he always seems to be bracing for something.

The causal loops tighten without him noticing. When a memory fragment intrudes—the bicycle, the smell, the sound of impact—he feels a surge of threat, and that threat makes him more likely to scan for triggers: the man standing too close, the bike locked outside the office window, the faint odor of alcohol from the break room. This scanning itself brings up more fragmented recall, because every familiar cue now feels like the prelude to violence. To manage the cycle, he drinks or smokes or simply avoids people altogether, but the substances and isolation amplify his startle reaction and his sense that he needs to monitor his surroundings even more carefully. He has taken to checking the locks on his apartment door three times before bed, certain that one slip-up could mean intrusion.

What finally brought Tui to seek help was the look on his girlfriend’s face when he flinched away from her father’s handshake last Sunday—a normal, friendly gesture, but the man’s size and the faint alcohol on his breath had sent Tui’s mind straight to the fragmented memory of his father’s arrival home. He knew then that his vigilance was costing him the relationships he wanted to keep. He is afraid that if he stops watching, the violence will find him again; but he is more afraid of losing the person who has been patient with his avoidance. That’s the fear that finally pushed him into the clinic.
